The Smallmouth yellowfish Labeobarbus aeneus is a potamodromous cyprinid endemic to the Orange-Vaal River system of southern Africa. Field surveys have documented that individuals attain a maximum recorded total length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], a size that positions this species among the larger members of its genus within the region. Mark-recapture studies suggest that under natural conditions, this length is achieved gradually over many years, reflecting the species' moderately paced growth trajectory. At the onset of gonadal development, typically associated with the transition to reproductive competence, the average total length at puberty has been measured at 28.9 cm [Lp = 28.9 cm]. This length is reached after a juvenile period that involves substantial somatic investment. When reared under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the time required from egg deposition to hatching is approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days]. This rapid embryonic development is typical of warm-water cyprinids and stands in contrast to the longer incubation periods observed in temperate congeners.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from the egg at a very small size, with the average wet weight at birth recorded at 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams]. This minute mass is derived from the modest egg diameter of roughly 1.3 mm and reflects a lecithotrophic strategy in which the alevin relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first days of life. The newly emerged prolarva is transparent and largely immobile, but within hours begins to exhibit sporadic swimming bursts. As the yolk-sac is progressively absorbed, the larva undergoes a trophic switch to exogenous feeding, marking a critical transition in early life history. The initial body mass is orders of magnitude smaller than the size attained at the onset of puberty, a disparity that underscores the intensity of the growth phase characterizing the juvenile period. Comparisons with other southern African Labeobarbus species indicate that this birth mass is consistent with the general pattern of small, pelagic egg production common among potamodromous cyprinids that spawn in flowing waters.

As the species progresses toward reproductive maturation, body mass increases substantially from the larval stage. The wet weight at puberty for Labeobarbus aeneus has been determined from population samples to be approximately 247 grams [Wwp = approximately 247 grams]. This body mass corresponds closely to the total length at puberty of 28.9 cm, reflecting a length-weight relationship that is typical for the genus. Fish at this mass have developed fully differentiated gonads and are physiologically capable of participating in spawning runs. The energy required to reach this mass from the 0.0012 gram hatchling involves a several-hundred-thousand-fold increase in wet weight, a feat accomplished through sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates and algae during the juvenile phase. Within the Orange River system, individuals attaining this mass typically begin to exhibit the migratory behavior associated with the spawning season, moving upstream in response to flow pulses. The ultimate wet weight reached by fully grown, senescent adults has been estimated at 1291 grams [Wwi = 1291 grams], representing the asymptotic body size beyond which little additional growth occurs.

Regarding the species' reproductive output, females of Labeobarbus aeneus that have attained the 247-gram pubertal mass are capable of substantial fecundity. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species' spawning season at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a single gravid female can produce approximately 557 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 557 eggs per spawning event] and typically spawns one to two times per year [F_R_i = one to two times per year]. This high fecundity is characteristic of a batch-spawning strategy in which multiple clutches of demersal, adhesive eggs are deposited over an extended breeding season. The combination of large clutch sizes and repeated spawning events allows a single female to contribute thousands of offspring annually, a life-history strategy that compensates for potentially high rates of early mortality in the planktonic larval stage. Field observations confirm that spawning aggregations form over gravel substrates in rocky riffles.

The lifespan of Labeobarbus aeneus under natural conditions is constrained by both environmental and physiological factors. Mark-recapture studies and otolith ageing have revealed that the maximum longevity documented for wild individuals is 12 years [am = 12 years], with this duration measured in populations inhabiting the Orange River at a mean water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This lifespan is relatively moderate for a cyprinid of its size, falling within the range observed for other large-bodied Labeobarbus species in southern Africa. The oldest individuals are typically those that have avoided both predation and fishing pressure, and they exhibit signs of reproductive senescence in their final years. The 12-year lifespan stands in contrast to much shorter-lived small cyprinids of the same region, which rarely exceed 3 to 5 years. This extended longevity allows for iteroparous reproduction across multiple breeding seasons, with females potentially participating in ten or more annual spawning runs over the course of their lives. The combination of a 6-day embryonic period, a 247-gram puberty mass, a 1,291-gram ultimate mass, and a 12-year lifespan describes a life-history strategy centered on moderate growth punctuated by high fecundity.
